problem: Quadruped robots are mostly taught isolated skills (locomotion, navigation) and lack a holistic agent. Existing adjustable-gait policies need manual behavior-parameter tuning, and prior navigation (GOAT) uses a closed-set segmenter and a fixed gait.
motivation: Pet-like agility combined with human-level cognition needs multimodal understanding, terrain-adaptive gaits with safe paths, and long-horizon planning. LMMs hold commonsense about gaits, terrain traversability and task decomposition, but are insensitive to precise numbers.
key_idea: Use GPT-4o as the brain of a quadruped that picks gait parameter ranges (validated by simulation, LSS), assigns open-vocabulary terrain and object costs for path planning, and decomposes instructions into skill calls.
insight: LMMs know which gait suits which terrain but are poor at exact numeric values. Having the LMM pick coarse ranges and then sampling and simulating to select the best parameters works better than direct prediction. In the Figure 4 ablation, Sampling beats Determining, which is unstable. In the appendix, adding detailed prior knowledge to the prompt (Auto+prior) hurts performance. LSS matches or beats expert tuning on most terrains and metrics, while manual non-expert tuning is worst.
method: Automatic locomotion adaptation (LSS): builds on Margolis et al.'s walk-these-ways adjustable policy with parameters b=[body height, step frequency, pitch, stance width, swing height, gait timing offsets]; the LMM outputs qualitative ranges (very low to very high).

Simulation and selection: candidate parameters are uniformly sampled within the ranges (e.g. body height step 0.05, frequency 0.2), rolled out in Isaac Gym, and the set with the highest linear-velocity tracking reward is chosen. For the real robot, the LMM also picks the matching simulated terrain.

2D open-vocabulary cost map: the LMM lists object and terrain categories from the RGB view. SEEM performs dense segmentation, which is projected with depth into a 3D voxel map and then a 2D map (5 cm cells). The LMM assigns costs in [0,1] using commonsense and the user instruction (0 to encourage a terrain, 1 to forbid it).

Navigation pipeline (GOAT-based): a global policy looks up goals in instance memory or explores by frontier; a local policy plans with the Fast Marching Method on the cost map. The Go2's built-in controller executes the offsets. LSS is re-invoked for a new gait when entering a new terrain.
Instance memory: clusters detections of objects and terrains by category and dilated map overlap into instances.
High-level reasoning: the LMM decomposes instructions into calls from a skill library (navigate_to(instruction), sit_down, lift_up_paw, shake_body, speaking) and executes them in order.

setting.backbone: GPT-4o (frozen) + SEEM segmentation + pretrained walk-these-ways adjustable locomotion policy
setting.training_data: none (training-free on the LMM side; reuses a pretrained RL locomotion policy)
setting.observation: egocentric RGB-D (RealSense D435i) plus onboard 2D position and RPY orientation
setting.action_space: velocity commands (vx, vy, wz) with adjustable gait parameters; waypoints from the cost-map planner; high-level skill calls

numbers.extra: average over 10 runs, 250-step episodes; metrics are percent of max episodic reward; Expert row: 70.08/75.68/95.44/94.15

numbers.eval_set_note: uphill slope and upward stairs, 5 runs each
numbers.extra: successes out of 5 runs; Uphill 4/5 (Fixed 2/5), Stairs 4/5 (Fixed 0/5)
numbers.evidence: Table 2: LSS 4/5 and 4/5 vs FIXED 2/5 and 0/5 (percentages computed from the printed fractions)

numbers_note: Locomotion results are on a self-built benchmark. Path planning and high-level reasoning are qualitative only (figures and video); no numeric navigation metrics are reported. The real-world SR values are computed from the printed fractions 4/5.
results: Auto+LSS beats manual tuning by large margins (e.g. downhill r_vxy 71.76 vs 44.52) and matches or exceeds expert tuning on most terrains (upward stairs 31.66 vs 29.44, downward stairs 61.97 vs 60.31, uphill slope 71.83 vs 70.08). In the real world, LSS succeeded 4/5 on both slope and stairs, versus 2/5 and 0/5 for the fixed gait. The cost map and long-horizon decomposition are shown qualitatively.
limitations: Navigation and reasoning are evaluated only qualitatively, with no quantitative metrics or baselines. There are also no independent module evaluations.
Perception quality (depth accuracy, segmentation) limits performance, and LSS depends on a pretrained adjustable-gait policy plus per-terrain simulation.
Real-world locomotion evaluation is tiny (5 runs per scenario).
